name: Affect heuristic
statement: How something feels stands in for how likely or how risky it is, so a judgement that looks like a calculation is often a reading of a mood.
meaning: The proposal is that people carry an affective tag on almost everything they think about, positive or negative, and consult it before they consult anything slower. Its sharpest prediction concerns risk and benefit. Finucane and colleagues argue that in the environment the two tend to be positively correlated, since an activity low in benefit would not be permitted if it were high in risk. In people's judgements they come out inversely related: whatever feels good is rated both more beneficial and less dangerous. A second prediction, from Rottenstreich and Hsee, is that feelings should matter most exactly where probability information is hardest to feel, which is at very long odds.

origin.who: Melissa Finucane, Ali Alhakami, Paul Slovic and Stephen Johnson
origin.note: Their paper is "The affect heuristic in judgments of risks and benefits". Slovic and colleagues set out the general account seven years later in the European Journal of Operational Research under the bare title "The affect heuristic".

evidence: Finucane and colleagues ran two experiments, only the first of which used time pressure. Study 1 had 54 first-year psychology students at the University of Western Australia rate 23 hazards for risk and for benefit, 28 of them against a clock and 26 with as much time as they wanted. Correlations calculated on each person's ratings across 21 items averaged -0.45 under time pressure and -0.33 without it, and the gap between the two means gave t(52) = 1.64, p = 0.05 one-tailed, which the authors called approaching significance. Study 2 gave undergraduates at the University of Oregon vignettes designed to raise or lower the perceived risk or benefit of nuclear power, natural gas and food preservatives. The attribute nobody had manipulated moved in the affectively matching direction, and the correlation across the resulting 12 data points was -0.75. That paper's method section reports 213 participants and its results section counts 219. Rottenstreich and Hsee supplied the probability prediction, offering 40 people a choice between a kiss from a favourite film star and fifty dollars, either as a certainty or at a 1% chance. Many Labs 2's account of that study gives 35% taking the kiss under certainty and 70% under the long shot.

replication.headline: Finucane's risk-benefit experiment held in two preregistered repetitions, while the long-odds prediction reversed direction across 7,218 people.
replication.detail: Many Labs 2 put the kiss-versus-money choice in the first of its two slates, which 60 samples ran, for 7,218 participants. Where the original found 70% choosing the affective option under low probability against 35% under certainty, the replication found 47% against 51%, an odds ratio of 0.87 and d = -0.08, 95% confidence interval -0.13 to -0.03, p = 0.002. The interval excludes zero, so this is a reversal rather than a null, and it is a small one. Klein and colleagues count it among three effects running opposite to their originals at p < .05, and it is not among those that clear the stricter p < .0001 line they also report. Of the 60 samples, 57 returned nothing, two reached significance in the reversed direction and one in the direction the original predicted. The original d was 0.74 from 40 people, with a 95% interval Many Labs 2 gives as below 0.001 to 1.74. Finucane's own Study 2 has gone the other way. Efendić, Chandrashekar, Feldman and four colleagues repeated it on MTurk and Prolific under preregistration, analysing 1,552 participants after exclusions. Running the original's analysis, the correlation between manipulated and unmanipulated attributes was r(10) = -0.87, 95% CI [-0.96, -0.59] in the American sample and r(10) = -0.84, 95% CI [-0.95, -0.50] in the British one. The low-benefit condition was the exception, where risk ratings did not shift.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490.

limits: What failed is one prediction from one paper, and the affect heuristic is broader than that paper. The inverse relationship between perceived risk and perceived benefit has survived repetition. Skagerlund, Forsblad, Slovic and Västfjäll report it in 2020 at r = -0.85 among the 187 people in their sample of 575 who rated both attributes, and at r = -0.77 among 41 students rating 64 activities in the laboratory. The time-pressure claim rests on less than that, a one-tailed t of 1.64 in 54 students, and Efendić and colleagues repeated Finucane's Study 2 rather than Study 1. Read the failure as a verdict on the probability-weighting prediction rather than on the idea as a whole. The original kiss study is worth looking at before treating the reversal as a surprise: with 40 participants its interval reached 1.74, so it was compatible with almost any effect size including none.
misreadings: The affect heuristic is often invoked as though any emotional influence on a judgement confirms it. That makes the idea unfalsifiable and is not what its authors proposed; the claim has specific predictions and at least one of them has now failed at scale. It is also frequently merged with the availability heuristic, since vivid things are both easy to recall and easy to feel, but those are separate mechanisms making separate predictions. And a heuristic is a shortcut rather than a mistake. Finucane and colleagues offered affect as a way of making judgement efficient when a decision is complex or mental resources are short, not as a source of error.
